brief.question: What were the main debates in the Australian parliament in 2010, and what positions did members and parties take? Debates that year included The mining tax, The NBN, Boat arrivals and Hospital reform.
brief.answer:
In 2010, the Australian Parliament was dominated by several contentious debates. The mining tax was a major point of conflict, with the government arguing that the tax reform was necessary to deliver better superannuation for working families, reduce the company tax rate, and fund infrastructure. Government members accused the opposition of acting as "mouthpieces" for mining magnate Clive Palmer, who they claimed had contributed $800,000 to the Liberal National Party. The opposition, in turn, was portrayed as opposing the tax on behalf of the mining industry.

The National Broadband Network (NBN) was another central issue. Government senators defended the legislation, arguing it would fix the structure of the telecommunications industry and allow competition to thrive by addressing Telstra's market position. They accused the opposition of shallow rhetoric about creating a new monopoly. The opposition, however, criticized the government for refusing to submit the $50 billion NBN to a full cost-benefit analysis by the Productivity Commission, a move they said had the support of business leaders and the Reserve Bank Governor.

Border protection and boat arrivals were also fiercely debated. The opposition moved a motion calling on the Prime Minister to explain the government's failure to protect Australia's borders, citing the arrival of 53 boats and 2,750 people since she became Prime Minister. A Coalition speaker argued the government had failed on border protection, citing 110 boat arrivals and 5,523 people arriving by boat in 2010 alone, and criticized the opening of new detention centres at Northam and Inverbrackie. In contrast, a motion on boat arrivals moved by Senator Hanson-Young was defeated in the Senate on 12 May 2010, with six votes in favour and 35 against.
